loText: Describe and identify examples of liquidity options and explain the impact of liquidity options on a bank’s liquidity position and its liquidity management process.
question:
A bank supervisor is reviewing the inventory of liquidity options reported by a Chinese commercial bank. The bank lists the following items:

I. Committed credit lines of CNY 8 billion granted to corporate clients.

II. Sight and savings deposits of CNY 30 billion.

III. Fixed-rate mortgages of CNY 12 billion that borrowers may prepay at any time.

IV. A committed credit line of CNY 5 billion received by the bank from another financial institution.

V. European call options on equities bought by the bank’s trading desk.

Which of the items are liquidity options sold by the bank, that is, short liquidity option positions?

options.A: I and II only
options.B: I, II and III only
options.C: I, II, III and IV only
options.D: I, II, III and V only

solution:
Supervisor’s review: which items are liquidity options sold by the bank.

**Concept and theory**

To identify a liquidity option, ask two questions: (1) does someone hold a right to receive cash from, or give cash to, the bank at predefined terms, with exercise driven by liquidity needs rather than profit; and (2) who holds the right?

| Item | Holder of the right | Bank’s position |
|---|---|---|
| Committed line granted to a client | Client (draws cash from the bank) | Short (GARP: “sells”) |
| Sight and savings deposits | Depositor (withdraws cash) | Short |
| Prepayable fixed-rate mortgage | Borrower (gives cash back early) | Short |
| Committed line received from another institution | Bank (draws cash) | Long |

question:
A risk consultant at an Australian bank is calculating the effect of a drawdown on a committed credit line after the borrower was downgraded. The consultant measures the financial impact as the difference between the contract spread and the borrower’s current market spread, applied to the amount drawn.

| Item | Value |
|---|---|
| Committed line notional (AUD m) | 450.00 |
| Amount drawn today (AUD m) | 280.00 |
| Contract spread over 3-month BBSW (%) | 1.20 |
| Borrower’s current market spread over BBSW (%) | 3.05 |
| Current 3-month BBSW (%) | 4.10 |
| Remaining life of the line (years) | 3.00 |

options.A: Liquidity outflow of AUD 280 million; annual financial gain of AUD 5.18 million
options.B: Liquidity outflow of AUD 450 million; annual financial loss of AUD 8.325 million
options.C: Liquidity outflow of AUD 280 million; annual financial loss of AUD 8.54 million

question: A member of the board risk committee of a Singapore bank asks how to assess the closure of a large savings account. A private banking client has withdrawn and closed a savings account of SGD 650 million that paid 1.20% a year. The bank had invested the balance in risk-free assets yielding 2.95% a year, which it now sells to fund the withdrawal. Which of the following statements best describes the impacts on the bank?

options.A: Liquidity outflow of SGD 650 million; financial gain of SGD 7.8 million a year, because the bank no longer pays the deposit rate on the closed balance.

Singapore bank: impacts of the closure of a large savings account.

GARP singles out the savings account as the case where the two impacts of exercise are most unequal. When a client closes a savings account:

- the **financial impact** is often quite small: it is the missing margin between the contract deposit rate and the rate the bank earns on reinvesting the received amounts (usually risk-free assets), or alternatively the cost of replacing the deposit with a new one at a higher rate;

question:
A member of the board risk committee of a U.S. bank is reviewing the following statements in the bank’s draft policy on managing liquidity options (credit lines, deposits and prepayable loans):

I. The financial effects of liquidity options can be hedged directly, although only partially, by a mixture of standard and statistical techniques.

II. The liquidity impact of liquidity options can be managed only by holding cash reserves, by constraining the allocation of assets towards liquid assets, or by easy access to credit lines.

III. Easy access to committed credit lines from other financial institutions amounts to a short position in liquidity options for the bank.

IV. Because the liquidity impact can be hedged with interest rate derivatives, a bank with a hedging programme does not need to hold liquidity reserves.

Which of the statements are correct?

options.A: I and II only
options.B: I, II and III only
options.C: I, II and IV only
options.D: II only

solution:
U.S. board review: how the financial and liquidity impacts of liquidity options are managed.

**Concept and theory**

Having split the effect of exercise into a liquidity impact and a financial impact, GARP assigns each a different management approach:

| Impact | How it is managed |
|---|---|
| Financial | Can be hedged directly, although only partially, by a mixture of standard and statistical techniques |
| Liquidity | Can only be managed by the liquidity tools analysed in the rest of the chapter: cash reserves, a constrained allocation of assets in liquid assets, or easy access to credit lines |

question: A senior risk analyst at a Japanese regional bank is validating the bank’s client pricing model and recommending improvements. The model charges clients for interest rate risk and credit risk, but assigns zero cost to the cash reserves, the liquid-asset buffer and the received credit lines that the bank holds against deposit withdrawals and credit line drawdowns. Which recommendation is most consistent with the reading?

options.A: No change is needed, because liquidity options are exercised for liquidity reasons and therefore carry no financial value that needs to be priced into client contracts.
options.B: Include the costs of these tools when pricing client contracts, using models that price both long and short liquidity options and jointly consider liquidity and financial aspects.
options.C: Price the liquidity options sold to clients with a standard option model capturing only the financial effect, since the liquidity impact is managed separately by treasury.
options.D: Charge the buffer cost only to borrowers that draw on credit lines, because depositors give cash to the bank and therefore do not hold any liquidity option.

solution:
Validating a client pricing model that ignores the cost of liquidity tools.

**Concept and theory**

GARP closes Section 7.2 with the consequences of liquidity options for the bank’s management process and pricing. The tools that manage the liquidity impact (cash reserves, a constrained allocation of assets towards liquid assets, easy access to credit lines) all imply costs. These costs “have to be properly accounted for” when pricing the contracts dealt with clients. Three implications follow:

1. Client products that embed short liquidity options (deposits, credit lines, prepayable loans) must carry a charge for the liquidity tools they require.

question: A junior risk analyst at an Italian bank is building the term structure of expected cash flows (TSECF). She has slotted EUR 2.4 billion of sight deposits at their contractual (overnight) maturity, committed credit lines granted to clients at zero usage, and fixed-rate mortgages at their contractual amortisation schedule, noting that the textbook TSECF example assumes that no liquidity options are embedded in deposits. Her manager asks how liquidity options should be reflected. Which response is most accurate?

options.A: Liquidity options should be left out of the TSECF and handled only in the term structure of liquidity generation capacity, since they are sources rather than causes of liquidity risk.
options.B: Since cash flows arising from liquidity options are stochastic, they cannot enter a term structure of expected cash flows and should be ignored until the options are exercised.
options.C: Cash flows should be adjusted for liquidity options with behavioural models for products such as sight deposits, credit line usage and mortgage prepayment, as these flows are stochastic.
options.D: Only the deposits need a behavioural adjustment; credit line usage and mortgage prepayments are fixed by contract, so their cash flows remain deterministic in time and amount.

solution:
Building the TSECF: how liquidity options should be reflected.

**Concept and theory**

The LO asks for the impact of liquidity options on the bank’s liquidity management process. In monitoring, the main tool is the term structure of expected cash flows (TSECF) and its cumulated version (TSECCF), built from the causes of liquidity: existing and forecast contracts from ordinary business.

GARP’s textbook example deliberately assumes that no liquidity options are embedded in deposits, so that every flow is deterministic in time and amount. question:
A junior risk analyst at an Australian bank is building the TSECF and the term structure of expected cumulated cash flows (TSECCF) for a simplified balance sheet (AUD million): assets are bonds 60 and loans 140; liabilities are deposits 90, bonds issued 80 and equity 30. Assets bear no default risk, no liquidity options are embedded in the deposits, and interest is ignored. The TSECF runs to the end of business activity (the bucket beyond 10 years).

| Item | Amount (AUD m) | Contractual maturity profile |
|---|---|---|
| Bonds held | 60 | 25 in year 1; 35 in year 3 |
| Loans | 140 | 40 in year 2; 40 in year 4; 60 in year 8 |
| Deposits | 90 | 40 in year 1; 50 in year 2 |
| Bonds issued | 80 | 30 in year 3; 50 in year 6 |
| Equity | 30 | no contractual expiry |
| Undrawn committed line received | 25 | available until year 5 (off balance sheet) |

Which of the following is closest to the TSECCF at year 6 and in the bucket beyond 10 years?

options.A: AUD −30 million at year 6; AUD 0 million beyond 10 years

options.C: AUD −30 million at year 6; AUD 30 million beyond 10 years

question:

| Month | TSECF (net) | TSECCF |
|---|---|---|
| 6 | 18 | 65 |
| 7 | −40 | 25 |

A board member asks how the month-7 figures should be interpreted. Which of the following answers is most accurate?

options.A: The bank faces an expected cash shortfall of JPY 40 billion in month 7 that must be funded with new liabilities, because the net balance of that date is negative.
options.B: The bank faces an expected cash shortfall of JPY 15 billion in month 7, the amount by which the month-7 net outflow exceeds the month-7 TSECCF.
options.C: On an expected basis, the month-7 net outflow is netted against the cash position built up by earlier inflows, leaving a cumulative position of JPY 25 billion and no expected shortfall at that date.

I. Includes the expected cash flows of all existing contracts on both sides of the balance sheet, including bonds issued and loans received by the bank.

question:
The treasurer of a US bank is reviewing a draft of the month-4 bucket of the TSECF prepared by a junior analyst. The analyst has entered three positive amounts:

I. USD 300 million from the planned rollover of certificates of deposit maturing that month, in line with the funding plan for ordinary business.

II. USD 500 million the treasury could raise by drawing a committed credit line received from another bank, should a cash gap appear.

III. USD 200 million the treasury could raise by selling unencumbered Treasury bonds, should a cash gap appear.

Which of the following treatments is most consistent with the reading?

options.A: Keep all three amounts, since each is a positive cash flow the bank expects to be able to obtain in month 4.
options.B: Keep II and III only, since rollovers belong to the new business category and are modelled outside the TSECF.
options.C: Keep I and II only, since unsecured funding always enters the TSECF, whereas asset sales belong to the liquidity generation capacity.
options.D: Keep I only, since II and III are sources of liquidity that feed the liquidity generation capacity and are kept out of the TSECF and the TSECCF.

solution:
US bank: which of three positive amounts belong in the month-4 TSECF bucket.

GARP organises liquidity risk measurement around two classes of factors. The causes of liquidity risk (Definition 7.4.1) are all factors referring to existing and forecast future contracts originated by the ordinary business activity of the institution; their flows can be positive or negative. question:
A senior treasury analyst at a Singapore bank reviews the expected profile below (SGD million). The month-3 short cash position has been covered with short-term interbank borrowing.

| Month | TSECF (net) | TSECCF |
|---|---|---|
| 3 | −170 | −120 |
| 4 | 150 | 30 |

A colleague proposes to lend the whole month-4 inflow to corporate clients for one year. Which of the following statements is NOT correct?

options.A: The month-4 inflow first offsets the short cash position created by earlier outflows, so the cumulative position at month 4 is SGD 30 million.
options.B: The full SGD 150 million month-4 inflow can be treated as free surplus, since liquidity monitoring only needs the net balance of cash flows on a given date.
options.C: Because the month-3 short position had to be financed in any case, typically with new liabilities, SGD 120 million of the month-4 inflow goes to repaying those debts.
options.D: Netting in the TSECCF works in both directions: earlier inflows can cover a later net outflow, and a later net inflow can cover a short position left by earlier outflows.

Singapore bank: interpreting a month-4 inflow that follows a negative month-3 TSECCF.

**Concept and theory**

GARP’s netting argument for the TSECCF works in both directions. The familiar direction: if on a given date the balance of inflows and outflows is net negative, it can be netted against a positive cash position originated by past inflows. The reverse direction is equally true: the bank can use a net positive inflow on a given date to cover a short cash position deriving from past outflows.

GARP attaches a condition to the reverse case. A short cash position does not simply wait to be filled; it must be financed in any case, typically with new liabilities.
